chunk_findings.detail: The default `**/*.txt` classifies every `.txt` file as documentation, not just wording. For example, if a review round reviewed `requirements.txt` (or a non-generated `snapshots/expected.txt` used by tests) and that file is edited after triage, the path matches `doc_globs`; `RP.ignorable`/`refine_stale_notes` can treat it as reviewed documentation and filter it out of `moved`, so the gate is considered fresh and `complete` emits no “different tree” warning. That hides an unreviewed dependency or test-oracle change, contradicting the knob’s own “Documentation files: wording, not code” definition.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:59 (`review.doc_globs` default)

chunk_findings.detail: The new docs exemption treats any change to a recorded path matching `doc_globs` as “not new work”, not just a wording-only content edit. For example, after a final review round whose `recorded` snapshot contains `docs/inventory.md`, a subsequent `git rm docs/inventory.md` makes `changed_paths` include `docs/inventory.md` and makes the current tree entries omit it. In `refine_stale_notes`, the path appears in `moved` because the recorded content differs from the current missing content, but `ignorable` returns `True` because `path in recorded` and the path matches a doc glob, so the “passed on a different tree” note is dropped. Thus `ddflow complete` can report no different-tree warning even though a reviewed documentation file was deleted, which is not the wording-only edit the change intends to suppress.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/reviewed_paths.py:ignorable

chunk_findings.detail: The test does not reproduce the reported failure sequence. The bug is that the doc was edited *after* triage had settled the round (and then a later `complete` saw a “different tree”). In this test, `docs/notes.md` is rewritten at lines 60–62 before `_settle(repo)` is called at line 63, so the edit is already part of the tree observed by triage. If the remaining defect is that a settled/passed round is invalidated by a later doc edit, or that `complete` still warns after the final pass, this test can pass while the bug is still present: it creates a failed review, edits the doc, settles, and only asserts the gate outcome, never running `ddflow complete` or checking a post-settle edit. A regression test for this bug must settle first, then edit the doc, and then assert the pass survives / complete does not warn.

chunk_findings.detail: The new deletion check only marks a reviewed documentation path as `gone` when a worktree path is available and `wt / p` does not exist. When `wt is None`, the code explicitly falls back to an empty `gone` set, so a moved documentation path is treated as surviving even if it has been deleted in the tree being checked. For example, a review round records `docs/inventory.md`; later `git rm docs/inventory.md` is made; if this different-tree check runs with `wt is None`, `_moved_paths` can still return `docs/inventory.md`, `gone` is empty, `RP.ignorable` matches `docs/**`, and the path is filtered out of `moved`, suppressing the warning. This contradicts the knob documentation’s stated fail-closed rule that a reviewed doc that was deleted still blocks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:502 (`gone` computation)

chunk_findings.detail: The docs exemption is still not limited to wording-only edits: it exempts any existing reviewed doc whose content changed, because the only extra guard is `path not in gone`, which only detects a missing file. For example, after a final review round records `docs/inventory.md` containing the inventory-table claim, a later edit that removes or materially changes that table (or `docs/security.md` changing “authentication is required” to “authentication is optional”) leaves the file present, so `gone` is false, `globs.match(path, "docs/**")` is true, and `ignorable(...)` returns true. `refine_stale_notes` then drops it from `moved`, so `complete` emits no “different tree” warning even though reviewed doc content was changed after the round. The previous probe fixed only `git rm`/deletion; it does not address this non-deletion content-edit case.

chunk_findings.detail: The second `refine_stale_notes` call is intended to model a reviewed documentation file that has been deleted after the final pass, but it passes `gone=()` after `docs/notes.md` has been unlinked. The companion unit test for `ignorable` establishes that a deleted reviewed path is rejected only when the path is present in the `gone` argument, and `refine_stale_notes` receives `gone` precisely so it can forward that information. With `gone=()`, this call presents the deletion to `refine_stale_notes` as just another changed path matching `docs/**`, the same input class as the preceding wording-edit case. Under that contract, the note is filtered as ignorable, the call returns `[]`, and the subsequent `(out,) = ...` unpacking fails (or the expected note is not named). A realistic complete call after the unlink would pass `{"docs/notes.md"}` as the `gone` argument, so this test does not actually reproduce the deletion symptom it claims to test.

chunk_findings.detail: The stated primary failure mode is not addressed by this change. The bug is that a combined review can place the documentation and the enforcing test in different chunks, so a reviewer reading only the documentation chunk claims the inventory table is unchecked even though `test_the_inventory_matches_the_ratchet_baseline` is present in the other chunk. The only `review.py` hunk shown here changes the post-round triage filter for moved paths by passing `doc_globs` and `gone` to `RP.ignorable`; it does not change how review chunks are built, how chunks are presented to the reviewer, or how a claim is correlated with tests found in other chunks. Given the original input (one doc change and one test change in the same item), `ddflow review` can still split them, and the reviewer can still misread the claim as unenforced. The new knob only prevents a later documentation edit from invalidating triage; it does not fix the chunked-review misread described in the intent.

chunk_findings.detail: The new docs exemption treats a reviewed doc as “not new work” whenever the path is still present in `entries`, so it suppresses removal of reviewed content, not just wording-only edits. Given a review round whose `recorded` snapshot contains `docs/inventory.md` with an inventory table, if after that round the file is truncated to empty (or the table is deleted leaving some non-empty text), `refine_stale_notes` computes `p in entries`, so `p` is not in `gone`. `ignorable` then sees `path in recorded`, `path not in gone`, and a matching doc glob, returns True, and the `moved` filter drops the path. `complete` therefore emits no “different tree” warning even though the reviewed doc content was removed, contrary to the docstring’s “removing reviewed content is new work.”

chunk_findings.detail: The test uses a fixed one-second `sleep` in the fake reviewer and then asserts `not seen.exists()` after `run_cli` returns. chunk_findings.detail: The background child is re-invoked as `[sys.executable, "-m", "ddflow", *argv]` while inheriting the current working directory. The launcher should re-invoke the same entry point/module in a controlled way rather than relying on `python -m ddflow` from the caller’s cwd.

If `cmd_review` ignores `--detach` when `--delta` is present and runs the review in the foreground, the `subprocess.run` call simply blocks until that foreground review finishes, then the gate outcome is passed and the test still passes. Unlike `test_detach_returns_at_once_while_the_review_keeps_running`, this test never asserts that the launcher returned while the detached pid was still alive, nor that output was streamed before completion, so the reported `--delta` “killed with no output” regression can remain undetected.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:test_a_detached_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher

chunk_findings.detail: `_alive` uses `os.kill(pid, 0)`, which succeeds for zombie processes. If the detached reviewer writes the `began` marker and then exits before the test checks liveness, and its parent does not reap it (for example, when the tests run under a PID namespace where the test process is PID 1 and does not reap orphaned grandchildren), `os.kill(pid, 0)` returns success and the assertion passes even though the review is no longer running. Thus the new liveness check can still pass when the detached review did not outlive the launcher, which is the behavior the assertion was added to catch.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_alive

chunk_findings.detail: The reviewer installed by `_setup` cannot record a pass after the new short-slow delta test. When the `slow` file exists, the script does `exec sleep ${S:-120}`; `exec` replaces the shell, so the following `echo 'STATUS: NO FINDINGS'` is never executed. In `test_a_detached_delta_review_records_passed_without_the_launcher`, the delta review writes `slow` containing `4`, so the detached reviewer writes `began`, sleeps, and exits silently without emitting the verdict that the test’s own reviewer uses to pass. If `_gate` reflects the current head, the test times out and fails; if the first foreground review’s passed outcome is still visible, the test passes without the detached `--delta` review ever recording a verdict. Either way, the regression test does not prove the `--delta` detached fix.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_detach.py:_setup

chunk_findings.detail: The change embeds a literal review verdict block, `STATUS: NO FINDINGS`, in the fake reviewer fixture. This is verdict text inside the reviewed change; tooling or a reviewer scanning the diff/test output for status blocks can mistake it for the change’s own review status. The review policy explicitly says such embedded verdict text is itself reportable.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new module-level `scope` is never invalidated when a previously folded name is rebound in a way `candidates_in` does not fold. For example, given module-level source:

```python
HOUR = 3600
HOUR += 1
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```

`HOUR = 3600` stores `scope["HOUR"] = 3600`, but `HOUR += 1` is an `ast.AugAssign`, which the loop ignores, so the scope remains stale. When `BUG_WINDOW_S` is folded, `_number` resolves `HOUR` to 3600 and reports `BUG_WINDOW_S` as 604800, even though the actual module-level value is 604801. The same stale-value problem occurs with a later non-foldable assignment such as `HOUR = int(...)` because `number is None` causes `continue` before clearing the target from `scope`. This can make the constants ratchet record a wrong value, misclassify a tunable, or miss a duplicate.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new module-level `scope` is never invalidated when a previously folded name is rebound in a way `candidates_in` does not fold. For example, given module-level source:

```python
HOUR = 3600
HOUR += 1
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```

`HOUR = 3600` stores `scope["HOUR"] = 3600`, but `HOUR += 1` is an `ast.AugAssign`, which the loop ignores, so the scope remains stale. When `BUG_WINDOW_S` is folded, `_number` resolves `HOUR` to 3600 and reports `BUG_WINDOW_S` as 604800, even though the actual module-level value is 604801. The same stale-value problem occurs with a later non-foldable assignment such as `HOUR = int(...)` because `number is None` causes `continue` before clearing the target from `scope`. This can make the constants ratchet record a wrong value, misclassify a tunable, or miss a duplicate.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new “do not leave a stale value” cleanup only pops top-level `ast.Name` targets, so a non-foldable tuple/list unpacking still leaves stale folded names. Given module-level source:
```python
HOUR = 3600
MIN = 60
HOUR, MIN = get_pair()
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```
`HOUR, MIN = get_pair()` is an `ast.Assign` whose `targets` list contains one `ast.Tuple`, not `ast.Name` nodes. `_number(value, scope)` returns `None`, so the new loop runs, but `isinstance(t, ast.Name)` is false for the tuple target and neither `HOUR` nor `MIN` is popped. The later `BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR` therefore still folds using the stale `HOUR = 3600` and can be reported as an unclassified constant, even though at runtime `HOUR` is rebound from `get_pair()` and may not be 3600. This is the same stale-scope class the change claims to fix, but it remains reachable through unpacking assignments.

chunk_findings.detail: `by_point.setdefault((point, claim), t)` makes the carried verdict depend on the first kept finding with a given `(file+function, claim)`, not on the latest or otherwise authoritative triage. The whole bug being fixed is that the same claim can reappear under a new digest when the line moves, so `kept` can contain multiple findings with the same point and claim but different settled verdicts. chunk_findings.detail:
`_rebindings` only drops stale scope entries for `AugAssign`, `For`/`AsyncFor`, and `Delete`, so a module-level name rebound by other top-level statements remains in `scope` and can be folded as if it still had its old value. For example, in source such as:
```python
HOUR = 3600
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
from math import pi as HOUR
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```
the `from math import pi as HOUR` statement is an `ast.ImportFrom`; `_rebindings` returns `[]`, so `scope["HOUR"]` remains `3600`. The second `BUG_WINDOW_S` assignment is therefore folded to `604800`, while at runtime it is `7 * 24 * math.pi` (about `527.8`). This misclassifies the symbolic arithmetic and can corrupt the constants ratchet. The same stale-scope problem also exists for other module-level rebinding forms such as `import`, `def`, `class`, `with` targets, `except` targets, walrus expression statements, and nested assignments inside module-level compound statements.

chunk_findings.detail: `by_point[(point, claim)] = t` selects the last kept finding with a given design point and claim, not the latest triage. If triage can be updated after findings are added, kept order does not equal triage recency. For example, `kept` is ordered `[D1, D2]`, both at `a.py:f` with claim `missing check`. `D2` was triaged `refuted` when it appeared, and later `D1` is re-triaged `confirmed`, making `confirmed` the latest verdict. The loop sets `by_point` from `D1` (`confirmed`) and then overwrites it with `D2` (`refuted`), so a delta re-raise inherits `refuted`. The previous first-vs-last fix does not answer this case because it still assumes the last item in `kept` is the latest authoritative triage.

The new `_rebindings` uses `ast.walk(node)` and treats every binding found anywhere inside a top-level statement as a module-scope rebind, including bindings inside function and class bodies. Those are not module-level rebinds. For example, given a module containing:

```python
HOUR = 3600.0

def _helper():
    HOUR = 1.0

BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```

when the audit processes the `def _helper`, `ast.walk` sees the local `Assign` to `HOUR`, `_rebindings` returns `HOUR`, and the module-scope `HOUR` is dropped. The later `BUG_WINDOW_S` is therefore no longer foldable and is not reported as a knob, even though at import time module-level `HOUR` is still `3600.0` and `BUG_WINDOW_S` is `604800.0`. The same false-negative behavior applies to class-body assignments, nested method/class names, imports, etc. This reintroduces the same class of problem the change is meant to fix: a real module-level tunable can be hidden from the constants ratchet.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new traversal only recurses into children that are `ast.stmt`, but an `ast.Try` node’s `handlers` are `ast.ExceptHandler` nodes, not `ast.stmt`, so bindings inside `except` blocks are skipped. For example, with:

```python
HOUR = 3600
try:
    1 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    HOUR = 1
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```

when the audit processes the top-level `try` statement, `_rebindings` never sees `HOUR = 1` in the handler. `scope["HOUR"]` remains `3600`, and the later `BUG_WINDOW_S` is folded as `604800`. But that handler assignment is a module-scope rebinding the audit must invalidate—the previous `ast.walk` would have found it, and the new docstring explicitly says `try` bodies are traversed—so a correct audit should drop `HOUR` and not classify `BUG_WINDOW_S` using the stale value.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_rebindings` only drops stale scope entries for `AugAssign`, `For`/`AsyncFor`, and `Delete`, so a module-level name rebound by other top-level statements remains in `scope` and can be folded as if it still had its old value. For example, in source such as:
```python
HOUR = 3600
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
from math import pi as HOUR
BUG_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```
the `from math import pi as HOUR` statement is an `ast.ImportFrom`; `_rebindings` returns `[]`, so `scope["HOUR"]` remains `3600`. The second `BUG_WINDOW_S` assignment is therefore folded to `604800`, while at runtime it is `7 * 24 * math.pi` (about `527.8`). This misclassifies the symbolic arithmetic and can corrupt the constants ratchet. The same stale-scope problem also exists for other module-level rebinding forms such as `import`, `def`, `class`, `with` targets, `except` targets, walrus expression statements, and nested assignments inside module-level compound statements.

chunk_findings.detail: The added entry whitelists `ddflow/services/swarm_metrics.py:BUG_WINDOW_S` as the `swarm.bug_window_s` knob instead of removing the duplicate the bug describes. chunk_findings.detail:
The new special case recurses into handler bodies only for `ast.Try`, not `ast.TryStar`. In Python 3.11+, a top-level `try/except*` has the same non-`ast.stmt` `ExceptHandler` nodes as `try/except`, so `ast.iter_child_nodes` will not visit their `body` statements and the `isinstance(node, ast.Try)` guard is false. try:
```python
    pass
except* ZeroDivisionError:
    HOUR = 1
A_WINDOW_S = 7 * 24 * HOUR
```

chunk_findings.detail: Locations with no colon, e.g. a file-level design point cited as `"README.md"` rather than `"path:line"` or `"path:func"`, are normalized to `""`. Because `_carry_delta_verdicts` skips entries with a false point, a prior triaged file-level finding can never be matched to the same finding in a later delta. Concretely, if `kept` contains `{"digest": "d1", "location": "README.md", "detail": "README says X"}` with settled triage `refuted`, and `mine` contains the same location/detail under a new digest `"d2"`, `_design_point("README.md")` returns `""`, so `by_point` remains empty and the new delta finding stays untriaged even though the cited file and claim are identical. The early `return ""` should be `return loc` for non-empty locations that merely have no colon.

chunk_findings.detail: `carried_set = set(carried)` takes the keys of `carried`. `_carry_delta_verdicts` is a mapping from the old digest whose verdict is being carried to the new digest the delta assigns to the re-raised design point (old → new). But `kept` contains the **new** digest. So for old digest `A` and new digest `B`, `carried_set == {"A"}` while the finding in `kept` has digest `B`; since `B` is not in `carried_set` and `verdicts` is the old folded triage without `B`, `_untriaged` still counts `B` as untriaged even though `_carry_delta_verdicts` just carried a settled verdict for it. Given the stated intent, the result should be 0, not 1. For the old→new mapping, this should be `set(carried.values())` (or otherwise check the new-digest side of the map).

chunk_findings.detail: The added regex `\bAIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}\b` will not redact a valid Google API key whose final suffix character is `-` when the key is followed by whitespace/punctuation or ends the text. Python `\b` only matches at a word/non-word transition, and both `-` and a following space are non-word. For example, `key = "AIza" + "f"*34 + "-"` in `session.prompt(log, cfg, sid, f"use key {key} and continue")` leaves the raw 39-character key on disk. Since `-` is in the pattern’s own allowed alphabet and gitleaks’ `gcp-api-key` rule (`AIza[0-9A-Za-z_-]{35}` without the trailing `\b`) would still flag this key, the CI failure this change is meant to fix can still occur. The added test only covers a key ending in `f`, so it does not exercise this case.

chunk_findings.detail: The new lease check calls `CK.verdict(repo, agent, paths, Path(p.cwd or Path.cwd()), refuse_no_lease=False)` without passing `root=repo`. `verdict` uses `root` to normalize path arguments for comparison against the repository-root-relative lease globs returned by `_mine(repo, agent)`, falling back to the tool cwd when `root` is omitted. Example: repo `/repo`, agent lease glob `subdir/**`, `p.cwd = /repo/subdir`, and a pre_tool call whose raw path is `/repo/subdir/out.txt`. With `root=None`, `_relative` normalizes the path against `/repo/subdir`, yielding `out.txt`, which does not match `subdir/**`; `verdict` returns `REFUSE` and the valid write inside the lease is denied. It should pass `root=repo` (and can also fail to match outside-lease paths correctly for non-root cwds).

chunk_findings.detail: The new trailing guard `(?![0-9A-Za-z_-])` is too strict and now fails to redact valid Google API keys when they are followed by a character in the base64url alphabet that the previous `\b` treated as a boundary. For example, `key = "AIza" + "Z" * 35` ends in a word character; in `session.prompt(log, cfg, sid, f"try {key}-suffix")` the regex sees the following `-`, which is in the negative lookahead class, refuses to match, and writes the raw `AIza...` key to the log. Likewise, a dash-ending key followed by `_` or a digit is no longer redacted. The new test only covers a following space, so it does not catch this regression.
